A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Knockout method and corresponding experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including identifying relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original regression and classification simulations and experiments on Alzheimer's forecasting, noisy-label learning, tumor segmentation, tree classification, and prostate cancer detection, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds further simulations, ablations, model configurations, and text-image classification experiments on UPMC Food-101.

M1.justification: Both versions use independent random masking, placeholder substitution, the same supervised objective, structured masking, and distinct placeholders for induced versus observed MAR/MNAR missingness. v3 clarifies sampling and evaluates additional model configurations; its new Knockout- variant ablates an existing component rather than revising the proposed method.

E1.justification: v3 adds text-image classification on UPMC Food-101 and controlled self-censored MNAR training scenarios, extending modality and missingness coverage. Conversely, v1's Buffalo Auto Arborist evaluation in Table S8 disappears. The prior Columbus results remain identifiable in v3 Table 5's ResNet-50 rows despite the omitted site label.

E2.justification: The regression comparison expands beyond the common baseline, missForest, and Knockout* to input dropout, zero imputation with indicators, MICE, MIWAE, supMIWAE, KNN, and linear-regression imputation. v3 also adds the out-of-support-imputation common baseline in mixed-input classification and Knockout* in the noisy-label comparison. Food-101 includes additional published comparator scores.

E3.justification: v3 retains the main 3,000-sample regression setting but adds 300-, 1,000-, and 15,000-sample evaluations, a self-censored MNAR protocol, and ViT-B-16 tree-classification configurations. Food-101 introduces a ResNet50/RoBERTa evaluation with its own training budget and validation split. Newly specified details of retained experiments do not establish that their procedures changed.

E4.justification: New analyses test training-data sensitivity, distinguishing observed MNAR missingness from induced masking, out-of-support imputation without Knockout training, and placeholder choice in noisy-label learning. The scalar placeholder sweep and structured-image placeholder analysis already existed in v1; their relocation or redisplay is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 explicitly identifies CIFAR variability as standard deviations; v3 Table 4 retains the same uncertainty values and five-run count but omits that identification. Otherwise, established repetition counts, Alzheimer's standard errors, and segmentation confidence intervals remain unchanged. There is no evidence of increased repetitions or new statistical testing.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for new comparators, MNAR experiments, training-size analyses, ViT configurations, and placeholder controls, while removing Buffalo results. Newly reported Food-101 accuracies are 92.7% versus 91.5% for the common baseline with both modalities, and 63.2% versus 47.5% with images alone. Existing main CIFAR scores and prostate AUCs are retained.

T1.justification: v3 corrects reversed mask states in Section 2.2's marginalization identity and Appendix A.2's derivation. It adds a positive-denominator assumption and a discrete counterexample demonstrating failure of an in-support placeholder. These are localized mathematical corrections and additions; the principal marginalization argument and multitask decomposition remain.

C1.justification: The central contribution—learning conditional and marginal predictors through placeholder-based augmentation—remains unchanged. However, Section 5 strengthens the empirical claim from consistently achieving competitive performance in v1 to consistently outperforming conventional imputation and ensemble methods in v3, despite exceptions in the reported results.

C2.justification: v3 adds finite-data versus asymptotic interpretations of imputation, discusses applicability to modern multimodal models, and identifies SGD-based training as a boundary. It removes v1's explicit caveat about untested missing-pattern-specific models. Its new claim that Knockout consistently beats Knockout- overstates Table 3: with three missing features, MSE is 0.175 versus 0.163.

D1.justification: v3 discloses the 0.0741 regression knockout rate, exhaustive testing of 130 missingness patterns, additional feature dimensions, and the Food-101 training recipe. These improve documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments. Conversely, it removes the CPU-testing hardware detail, specific ADNI application instructions, and the retained tree results' site identification.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against imputation theory and supervised missing-data research, including Josse, Bertsimas, Le Morvan, and Ipsen. It acknowledges closely related masking approaches by Neverova and Parthasarathy and Sundaram, and discusses modern multimodal and foundation models. These additions materially qualify the relationship to prior work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental descriptions, and ADNI appendix undergo widespread rewriting. Placeholder guidance and comparator descriptions gain structured lists and expanded explanations; Section 5 becomes a broader Discussion. The main experimental narrative now explicitly develops analyses previously presented primarily in appendix figures.

P2.justification: v3 changes typography, author layout, spacing, and table organization throughout. Regression plots expand to three panels with larger comparator legends; the tree table gains backbone groups. New summary, ablation, and Food-101 displays are added, Buffalo's table is removed, and the Gaussian illustration and placeholder sweep move into the main text.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation of the unchanged method: its much broader regression comparisons address v1's limited comparator coverage, while controlled MNAR, training-size, and augmentation controls directly examine important assumptions. Corrected mask identities and closer engagement with prior work also improve the scientific argument. Dropping Buffalo results and the missing-pattern-specific baseline caveat reduces completeness, and the Table 3 interpretation overclaims superiority. Nevertheless, the expanded comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement in the paper's support and assessability.
